title: Ollama serve fails to detect Nvidia GPUs after updating to the latest version
body: After updating Ollama from 0.11.11 to 0.12.5 on Windows 11 Enterprise 25H2 without Docker, `ollama serve` no longer detects my NVIDIA GPUs and reports only CPU inference with 0 B VRAM. Older 0.11.11 logs show that the GPUs were detected. I tried setting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2, but it still falls back to CPU.

symptoms_visible: After updating from Ollama 0.11.11 to 0.12.5, `ollama serve` detects only the CPU, reports 0 B VRAM, and enters low-VRAM mode even though older logs show my NVIDIA GPUs.
N0.label: N0 GPU discovery regression reported

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.12.5 still reports only CPU inference after I remove CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, while `nvidia-smi` lists all three GPUs and other CUDA applications can use them.
N1.label: N1 environment override ruled out

symptoms_visible: With Ollama 0.11.11 installed again, startup lists my GPUs, but every model I try still loads into RAM and runs on the CPU.
N2_x.label: N2_x downgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.12.6 still detects no GPUs after I reinstall the NVIDIA software stack, reinstall Ollama, and try a simplified PATH.
N3_x.label: N3_x software reinstall aftermath

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.12.9 on my Windows 11 Enterprise 25H2 installation prints `The specified procedure could not be found` for every ggml CPU library and for `cuda_v12\ggml-cuda.dll`.
The same GPUs work with Ollama inside a Windows 11 24H2 Sandbox and on a clean Enterprise 24H2 installation, while the failure appears again after that clean installation is updated to 25H2.
N4_x.label: N4_x dynamic library load failure isolated

symptoms_visible: A bare 25H2 installation without third-party antivirus still fails to load the Ollama libraries.
N4b.label: N4b antivirus ruled out on a bare 25H2 install

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.13.0 finally lists my GPUs, but models still load into system RAM and use about 70–80% CPU instead of VRAM.
When I start `ollama serve`, all four monitors go black briefly as if the NVIDIA display driver has restarted.
N5_x.label: N5_x 0.13.0 partial improvement aftermath

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.13.0 still loads models into system RAM and uses the CPU even though startup now lists the GPUs.
N6.label: N6 conflicting PATH copy checked

symptoms_visible: After I copied the `ggml-base.dll` from the Ollama installation folder to `C:\Windows`, all my models load into the VRAM of my GPUs.
N7.label: N7 release DLL made resolvable, VRAM loading restored

symptoms_visible: With the system-wide copy removed and Ollama loading the `ggml-base.dll` from its own installation folder, my models still load into the GPUs' VRAM and inference runs on the GPUs.
N_terminal.label: terminal GPU inference restored

question_patterns: Quit Ollama, unset CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, run `ollama serve` with OLLAMA_DEBUG=2, and share the log once it reports inference compute.
Does GPU discovery still fail in a debug run with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES removed?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I removed CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, set OLLAMA_DEBUG=2, and ran `ollama serve`. It still ends with only `inference compute id=cpu`; reinstalling Ollama did not change it.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: After removing CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, the debug run detects all three GPUs and models use VRAM normally.
The same CPU-only result occurs when I use the GPU UUIDs instead of indices.

question_patterns: Can you share the output of `nvidia-smi`?
Which GPUs and NVIDIA driver does the machine report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My `nvidia-smi` output lists an RTX 5070 and two RTX 3060 cards, all in WDDM mode, with driver 581.57 and CUDA 13.0.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: `nvidia-smi` cannot communicate with the NVIDIA driver and does not list any GPUs.

edges.comment: Reporter supplied debug output with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES removed and raw nvidia-smi output. This rules out the numeric visibility override as the primary cause and establishes that the NVIDIA driver can enumerate the hardware.

solution.intent: Downgrade to Ollama 0.11.11 because that version previously enumerated the GPUs.
solution.concrete_example: Uninstall 0.12.5, reinstall 0.11.11, and retry a small model.

edges.comment: Actual attempted rollback: 0.11.11 enumerated the cards but still loaded models into RAM and executed on the CPU, so enumeration alone was not sufficient.

solution.intent: Refresh the installed Ollama and NVIDIA/CUDA software stack and retry with Ollama 0.12.6.
solution.concrete_example: Remove and reinstall the NVIDIA components and CUDA runtimes, reinstall Ollama 0.12.6, and retry with a simplified PATH.

edges.comment: The reporter used NVIDIA CleanUpTool, reinstalled CUDA releases and Ollama, and simplified PATH. Ollama 0.12.6 still failed to discover the GPUs.

solution.intent: Update to Ollama 0.12.9 with enhanced loader diagnostics and compare the behavior in clean Windows environments.
solution.concrete_example: Install 0.12.9, run with OLLAMA_DEBUG=2, and compare its backend-loading output with a clean Windows Sandbox or installation.

edges.comment: 0.12.9 did not restore GPU use, but its added diagnostics exposed raw `The specified procedure could not be found` errors for every CPU backend and the CUDA backend. The reporter also independently compared Sandbox, clean 24H2, upgraded 25H2, and bare 25H2 environments.

question_patterns: Could another piece of software be intervening — do you run any third-party antivirus or endpoint protection on that machine? If so, can you disable it temporarily, or test an installation without it, and tell me whether the libraries load?
Does the load failure still happen on a 25H2 installation that has no third-party security software on it?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No, I'm not in a corporate environment - it's my own personal computer. I installed a bare Windows 11 Enterprise edition, without any AV software or anything else; the Ollama setup EXE installed vc_redist.x64.exe, but nothing else. Despite this, Ollama fails to detect my GPUs. (MsMpEng.exe does spin up during the initial loading of a model, but that is part of Windows Security.) Perhaps the updates have something to do with the libs not being loaded? My firmware was also updated from 2006 to 2009.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: With my security software disabled the libraries load without error and Ollama detects all three GPUs again.
MsMpEng.exe spikes while Ollama starts, but an installation with no third-party AV fails in exactly the same way.

edges.comment: Maintainer-initiated measurement: he asked whether AV or endpoint software could be blocking the DLLs. The reporter answered from a bare 25H2 installation carrying no third-party AV, which still failed, and attached his Windows-update and firmware-version screenshots to that same answer. Kept as a clarification (not volunteered) because the engineer asked for it.

solution.intent: Install Ollama 0.13.0 and retry GPU discovery and model loading.
solution.concrete_example: Update to 0.13.0, start `ollama serve`, and load a model while watching system RAM, CPU usage, and GPU VRAM.

edges.comment: 0.13.0 improved enumeration, but it did not resolve inference: models still used RAM and CPU, and starting the server visibly reset the display driver.

question_patterns: Can you search PATH and system-wide locations for another `ggml-base.dll` that could conflict with Ollama's copy?
Is there another copy of `ggml-base.dll` somewhere Windows may load before the one in the Ollama installation?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No, there are no other `ggml-base.dll` files in PATH. ComfyUI, SwarmUI, Whisper, and my other tools are all in their own folders outside PATH.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I found an older `ggml-base.dll` in a system directory, and removing it made Ollama load models into VRAM again.
I found no duplicate in PATH, but there are unrelated ggml libraries inside application-private folders.

edges.comment: The maintainer asked the reporter to look for a conflicting copy of ggml-base.dll. The reporter's raw answer was that no other copy existed in PATH; interpreting the later successful placement experiment as a DLL search or resolution failure remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Ollama loads its `ggml-*.dll` backends dynamically at runtime, so the loader still has to find the `ggml-base.dll` they depend on. As a test, can you make the `ggml-base.dll` from your current Ollama installation resolvable from a location the Windows loader always searches, restart `ollama serve`, load a model, and tell me whether it goes into VRAM or still into RAM?
Can you try making the `ggml-base.dll` that ships with your installed Ollama build visible to the Windows DLL search path, and then report whether models load into GPU VRAM?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I've finally fixed it!! I copied `ggml-base.dll` from the Ollama installation folder to `C:\Windows` and now all the models are loading to VRAM of my GPUs!

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I put the current `ggml-base.dll` where Windows searches, restarted the server and loaded a model, and nothing changed - it still loads into RAM and runs on the CPU.
Models load into VRAM now, but `ollama serve` still makes my monitors go black once when it starts.

edges.comment: Measurement-class probe. The reporter made the current installation's ggml-base.dll resolvable by copying it to C:\Windows and reported only what he then observed: models loading into VRAM. Reading that as proof of a DLL-resolution failure, and knowing that a system-wide copy is not a safe permanent configuration, is engineer-side and lives on the following solution edge. The destination is intentionally not flagged user_perceives_resolved even though the reporter celebrated here: that marker ends the episode, and the thread's accepted answer still had to be delivered afterwards.

solution.intent: Correct the Windows DLL-resolution failure so Ollama's backend libraries load the matching `ggml-base.dll` from the same Ollama release; treat the reporter's system-wide DLL placement only as a diagnostic workaround and verify actual VRAM use.
solution.concrete_example: The reporter's successful experiment was to copy the current installation's `ggml-base.dll` to `C:\Windows`, after which models loaded into VRAM. That points to a DLL lookup/loading problem rather than CUDA visibility. Do not keep that as the durable configuration: a system-wide copy can become stale and binary-incompatible on the next Ollama update. Ensure the loader resolves the same-release `ggml-base.dll` from Ollama's installation directory, remove system-wide copies, and retest a model while checking VRAM.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied raw loader errors, environment comparisons, the absence of another PATH copy, and the outcome of making `ggml-base.dll` visible from a system search location. Concluding that the common dependency was being resolved incorrectly—and that this explains both CPU and CUDA backend failures—is engineer-side inference. The copy to `C:\Windows` confirms the dependency path but is not a safe permanent deployment because `ggml-base.dll` changes between releases.

edges.comment: The reporter restored VRAM loading by copying the current ggml-base.dll to C:\Windows. The maintainer warned that a system-wide copy is binary-incompatible across releases and should be removed in favor of resolving the matching DLL from the Ollama installation directory.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the technical root cause as a Windows dynamic-library resolution/loading failure involving Ollama's matching `ggml-base.dll` and backend `ggml-*.dll` files, rather than failure of NVIDIA hardware enumeration or CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: all CPU and CUDA backends returned `The specified procedure could not be found`, the GPUs worked in other applications and clean 24H2 environments, and making the current `ggml-base.dll` visible through a Windows search location restored VRAM loading.

Must not present downgrading, reinstalling CUDA or NVIDIA drivers, simplifying PATH, changing CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, or merely updating to a newer Ollama release as the fix; each was tried without restoring GPU inference.

Must not recommend leaving `ggml-base.dll` in `C:\Windows` as a durable fix. It may be described as the reporter's successful diagnostic workaround, but the response must warn that system-wide copies can become stale and binary-incompatible after an Ollama update.
Must ask the user to verify that a model actually loads into GPU VRAM and uses GPU inference before declaring resolution; detecting the GPUs at startup alone is insufficient.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly persistent and technically capable power user who manages multiple NVIDIA GPUs, CUDA installations, Windows Sandbox and WSL2, can collect verbose logs, inspect DLL dependencies, modify environment variables, and compare clean operating-system installations.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, appreciative, and highly responsive; posts extensive logs and exact test results, tries many hypotheses independently, and expresses frustration or relief openly with emphatic wording and emoji.
